title: A hot knee in a man who 'just has gout'
presentation: A 58-year-old man presents with 36 hours of a severely painful, hot, swollen right knee. He cannot bear weight. He tells triage 'it's my gout again, I just need the tablets'. He has had two previous attacks of podagra. Triage: T 38.4 C, HR 102, BP 128/78, SpO2 97% on air.

stages.label: History
stages.text: Both previous gout attacks were in the right first MTP joint and settled within a week on colchicine. He was started on allopurinol 100 mg daily a year ago but ran out four weeks ago and has not refilled it. Past history: type 2 diabetes (metformin, HbA1c 8.2% last month), hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide, chronic kidney disease stage 3 (baseline eGFR 48). He drank several beers at a barbecue three days ago. No trauma. Yesterday evening he had rigors. No urethral discharge, no diarrhoea, no rash, no tick exposure, no recent travel, no intravenous drug use, no recent dental work or skin infection that he has noticed. No other joints are painful.
stages.prompt: What is your differential for an acute hot monoarthritis in this man, and what is the one thing you must do before any treatment?
stages.learner_goal: Build the hot-joint differential (septic, gout, pseudogout, less likely reactive, haemarthrosis) and recognise that aspiration is mandatory before antibiotics or steroids.

stages.label: Exam and aspiration
stages.text: T 38.6 C, HR 104. He looks unwell and is sweaty. The right knee has a large tense effusion, is warm and erythematous, and is held in about 20 degrees of flexion; any attempted movement causes severe pain. The skin over the knee is intact with no wound, no cellulitis extending beyond the joint, and no prepatellar swelling. No tophi on the ears, hands, or elbows. No other joint is inflamed. No heart murmur, no splinter haemorrhages, no skin lesions, dentition poor. The knee is aspirated under aseptic technique: 45 mL of turbid yellow fluid.
stages.prompt: What do you send the fluid for, and what else do you send before any drug goes in? Which result decides whether this is 'just gout', and what will you do while you wait?
stages.learner_goal: Send synovial fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and polarised crystal microscopy; take blood cultures; recognise that crystals do not exclude infection.

available_tests.synovial fluid crystals: Polarised microscopy: abundant needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent crystals, intracellular and extracellular (monosodium urate)
available_tests.synovial fluid gram stain: Gram stain: moderate Gram-positive cocci in clusters
available_tests.blood cultures: Two sets drawn before antibiotics; pending
available_tests.knee x-ray: Right knee radiograph: large effusion, no fracture, no chondrocalcinosis, no erosions, no periosteal reaction

stages.label: Results
stages.text: Synovial fluid: WBC 68,000/microlitre with 92% neutrophils. Polarised microscopy shows abundant needle-shaped, strongly negatively birefringent intracellular crystals. Gram stain: moderate Gram-positive cocci in clusters. Culture pending. Blood: WBC 15.2, CRP 190, ESR 70, serum urate 7.1 mg/dL, creatinine 1.7 mg/dL (eGFR 43). Knee radiograph: effusion only, no chondrocalcinosis. At 14 hours the microbiology laboratory telephones: both blood culture sets are growing Gram-positive cocci in clusters.
stages.prompt: The crystals are there. Is this gout? Commit to a diagnosis and tell me exactly what happens in the next six hours.
stages.learner_goal: Diagnose septic arthritis coexisting with gout, start intravenous anti-staphylococcal antibiotics now that cultures are taken, and refer for joint drainage.

stages.label: Day 2
stages.text: Synovial fluid and both blood cultures grow methicillin-sensitive Staphylococcus aureus. Orthopaedics performed an arthroscopic washout overnight. He is afebrile this morning, HR 88. Creatinine 1.6 mg/dL. The knee remains painful and he asks whether he can have 'the usual' ibuprofen, and whether he should restart his allopurinol.
stages.prompt: Finalise the plan: antibiotic choice and duration, what else the bacteraemia obliges you to look for, how you will treat the gout component in a man with an eGFR of 43, and what you do about the allopurinol.
stages.learner_goal: Narrow antibiotics, plan duration and source assessment for S. aureus bacteraemia, treat the gout flare without NSAIDs or intra-articular steroid, and address urate-lowering therapy.

diagnosis: Septic arthritis of the knee due to Staphylococcus aureus with coexisting acute gout
key_clues: Fever 38.6 C and rigors with a single hot joint
Risk factors for septic arthritis: diabetes, CKD, prior joint damage from gout, age over 50
Gram-positive cocci in clusters on synovial fluid Gram stain
Monosodium urate crystals present, which prove gout but do not exclude infection
Serum urate 7.1 mg/dL after stopping allopurinol (urate may be normal or low during a flare and does not decide anything)

distractors.name: Acute gout flare alone
distractors.why_not: Crystals are present, but fever of 38.6 C, rigors, Gram-positive cocci on the Gram stain, and positive blood cultures mean the joint is infected as well.

distractors.name: Pseudogout (CPPD arthritis)
distractors.why_not: The crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent (urate), not rhomboid and weakly positive; no chondrocalcinosis on radiograph.

distractors.name: Gonococcal arthritis
distractors.why_not: No urethritis, no migratory arthralgia or pustular skin lesions; the organism is Gram-positive cocci in clusters, not Gram-negative diplococci.

distractors.name: Reactive arthritis
distractors.why_not: No preceding enteric or genitourinary infection, and the synovial fluid culture is positive.

distractors.name: Haemarthrosis
distractors.why_not: No trauma, no anticoagulant, normal coagulation, and the fluid is turbid yellow, not bloody.

distractors.name: Prepatellar bursitis or cellulitis
distractors.why_not: The effusion is intra-articular with range of motion limited in every direction; bursitis spares passive flexion and there is no prepatellar swelling.

rubric.description: Names septic (infective) arthritis in the differential at the history stage
rubric.concept: An acute hot monoarthritis is septic arthritis until proven otherwise, whatever the past history

rubric.description: States that the joint must be aspirated before any treatment
rubric.concept: Aspirate every hot joint before antibiotics or steroids; the fluid is the diagnosis

rubric.description: Sends synovial fluid for cell count, Gram stain, culture, and polarised crystal microscopy
rubric.concept: The four synovial fluid tests: cell count with differential, Gram stain, culture, crystals
Blood cultures are positive in 30-50% of non-gonococcal septic arthritis and must be drawn before the first antibiotic dose

rubric.description: Explicitly states that finding crystals does not exclude infection, or that gout and septic arthritis can coexist
rubric.concept: Crystals and bacteria coexist in a small but real fraction of hot joints; a positive crystal result never closes the infection question

rubric.description: Final diagnosis is septic arthritis (with or without naming the coexisting gout)
Starts intravenous anti-staphylococcal antibiotics (empiric vancomycin pending sensitivities, then flucloxacillin, cefazolin, or nafcillin for MSSA)
rubric.concept: Empiric cover for S. aureus including MRSA until sensitivities return, then narrow; typically 2 weeks IV then oral to complete 4-6 weeks

rubric.description: Refers for joint drainage (arthroscopic washout or serial aspiration)
rubric.concept: Source control: a septic joint is a closed-space infection that needs drainage, not just antibiotics

rubric.description: Treats the gout component with renally adjusted colchicine or systemic steroid, avoids NSAIDs and intra-articular steroid, and addresses allopurinol
rubric.concept: Flare treatment in CKD: low-dose colchicine or oral prednisolone; never inject steroid into an infected joint; continue or restart allopurinol with flare prophylaxis

management_summary: This is Staphylococcus aureus septic arthritis with bacteraemia in a joint that also has acute gout. After blood and synovial cultures are taken, start intravenous vancomycin empirically (MRSA cover in a diabetic with CKD), then switch to flucloxacillin or cefazolin once MSSA is confirmed; plan about two weeks intravenously then oral therapy to complete four to six weeks, guided by response. Orthopaedic referral for arthroscopic washout the same day. S. aureus bacteraemia requires repeat blood cultures to document clearance and an echocardiogram to exclude endocarditis. Do not give NSAIDs (eGFR 43, diabetes) and do not inject steroid into the joint. Treat the gout component with low-dose colchicine (0.5 mg once daily given his CKD) or a short course of oral prednisolone once infection is under control, and restart allopurinol with colchicine prophylaxis before discharge, titrating to a urate below 6 mg/dL. Review the thiazide.
teaching_points: Every acute hot monoarthritis is septic until the synovial fluid says otherwise. A history of gout raises the probability of gout; it does nothing to lower the probability of infection, and a gouty joint is a damaged joint that is easier to infect.

Tap before you treat. Antibiotics given before aspiration can sterilise the fluid; steroids given into an infected joint are a disaster. The only reasons not to tap are overlying cellulitis or a prosthetic joint, and both mean orthopaedics tap it instead.

Interpret the fluid probabilistically. A synovial WBC above 50,000 raises the likelihood of infection but overlaps with crystal arthritis; the Gram stain is only 50-60% sensitive and culture 80-90%, so a negative Gram stain with a convincing clinical picture still gets treated as septic. Crystals and bacteria can occupy the same joint.

Fever and rigors with a hot joint earn blood cultures, and a positive S. aureus blood culture earns an echocardiogram, repeat cultures, and a longer antibiotic course. Treat the gout with agents that respect the kidneys, and do not stop urate-lowering therapy during a flare.
